This medicine is used as an adjunct in the treatment of chronic polyarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, arthropathy, ankylosing spondylitis, painful swelling or inflammation after trauma and surgery, and infections accompanied by inflammation, pain, and fever.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used as an adjunct in the treatment of chronic polyarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, arthropathy, ankylo

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201702324. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults take 1 capsule (300 mg) at a time, 2 to 4 times a day. However, do not exceed 4 capsules (1,200 mg) a day.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious, potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, patients with or a history of gastrointestinal ulcer, patients with bleeding in the gastrointestinal tract, the cerebral blood vessels, or other sites, severe blood disorders, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma or a history of it, those who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or an allergic reaction to aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients being treated for pain before or after coronary artery (heart artery) bypass graft surgery (CABG), pregnant women at 6 months of pregnancy or later, nursing mothers, patients with inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, and those who have experienced gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation from previous treatment with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with or a history of blood disorders, patients with a bleeding tendency, patients with or a history of liver disorder or kidney disorder, patients with fluid retention (accumulation of body fluid) or heart failure, patients with high blood pressure, those who have experienced hypersensitivity, patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), elderly people, children aged 6 years and older, patients with stomach cancer or alcoholism, pregnant women in early or mid pregnancy and women who may be pregnant, patients with ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease, or risk factors for cardiovascular disease (e.g., high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking), patients with hepatic porphyria, patients who have had major surgery that caused blood loss, patients with a blood coagulation disorder or who are receiving anticoagulants, and those who have experienced hypersensitivity or an allergic reaction to Yellow No. 5 should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Considering the importance of the drug treatment, either stop breastfeeding or stop taking the drug.
  • Dizziness or fatigue may occur after taking this medicine, so be careful when driving or operating machinery.
  • When it is taken for a long period for an acute illness, in principle this should be limited to within 5 days.

Possible side effects

  • If the following occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rarely shock (chest discomfort, chills, difficulty breathing, lowered blood pressure, etc.); rarely blood disorders such as aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, agranulocytosis, pancytopenia, thrombocytopenia, decreased platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), and eosinophilia; indigestion, abdominal distension, heartburn, upper abdominal pain, diarrhea or constipation; occasionally loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or stomach discomfort; rarely esophagitis, esophageal stricture, worsening of diverticula, nonspecific hemorrhagic colitis, ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, bloody stools, gastritis, or pancreatitis; very rarely thirst, stomatitis, erythema multiforme, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), or hair loss; occasionally angioedema; rarely Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome); drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency; occasionally rash, urticaria, itching, or purpura; rarely induction of an asthma attack, eczema, anaphylactic reactions, or photosensitivity reactions; rarely jaundice, elevated ALT, elevated AST, elevated ALP, abnormal liver function, hepatitis, or jaundice; occasionally rhinitis, bronchospasm, or acute pneumonia; rarely visual disturbances such as impaired vision and dark spots, hearing loss, tinnitus, or taste abnormality; fatigue, drowsiness, headache, or dizziness; occasionally anxiety, restlessness, confusion, or depression; rarely aseptic meningitis, severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness; rarely mental abnormality, agitation, excitement, disorientation, or reversible toxic amblyopia; rarely lowered blood pressure, raised blood pressure, palpitations, oliguria, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath, or languor; rarely renal papillary necrosis, nephrotic syndrome, interstitial nephritis, peripheral edema, acute pulmonary edema, fluid retention, hypertension, heart failure, or reduced fertility in women; occasionally periorbital edema; very rarely malaise, fever, nosebleed, or worsening of inflammation.

Interactions

  • Do not take together with aspirin, other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, or high-dose methotrexate used in cancer chemotherapy (15 mg/week or more).
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if you are taking corticosteroids, alcohol, digoxin, phenytoin, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, sulfonylureas, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists, diuretics, lithium, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), baclofen, immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, sirolimus), thrombolytics, ticlopidine, antithrombotic agents, medicines that increase blood potassium levels (trimethoprim, heparin, etc.), inducers of CYP2C8 or CYP2C9 (e.g., rifampicin, phenobarbital), low-dose methotrexate (less than 15 mg/week), antiplatelet agents, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, if you take low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke, or if you have experienced hypersensitivity or an allergic reaction to Yellow No. 5.

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold (sore throat, cough, phlegm, chills (feeling cold and sh

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201309431. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults and those aged 15 years and older take 1 packet per dose, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. If necessary, take it at bedtime, and keep the interval between doses at 4 hours.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, children under 2 years of age, and people who are taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian drugs, etc.) or are within 2 weeks of stopping them must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, those with an allergic constitution, those who have experienced allergic symptoms to medicines (e.g., fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, swelling, or gastroduodenal ulcer, elderly people, people who are physically weak, people with a high fever or with persistent or recurring stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain or with ulcer or bleeding problems, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and nursing mothers, and patients who smoke or have asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough lasting or recurring for 1 week or longer, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash, or persistent headache should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness (congested and reddened), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, swelling, dizziness, rarely shock symptoms (hives, swelling, and chest tightness immediately after taking it, together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing), skin-mucosa-eye syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (accompanied by high fever, with severe symptoms such as congestion and reddening and burn-like blisters appearing on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes), asthma, general lethargy, jaundice, interstitial pneumonia (dry cough, fever, etc.), decreased urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, a rise in blood pressure, headache, or myopathy (weakness, cramps in the limbs, paralysis) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take together with antitussives and expectorants (phlegm medicines), other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol, potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, etacrynic acid) or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide), diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, or steroids.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.

How it works

This medicine is used for fever and pain due to colds, headache, neuralgia, muscle pain, menstrual pain, and pain from s

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Children aged 12 years and under take the following recommended 1-time dose every 4 to 6 hours as needed. For the recommended 1-time dose by age group, refer to the approved labeling. Take the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible period, and do not take it more than 5 times a day (75 mg/kg). If the body weight is known, it is more appropriate to take a dose based on body weight (10 to 15 mg/kg).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported, and if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily amount of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products that contain acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood disorders, liver disorder, kidney disorder, or reduced cardiac function, and patients with aspirin-induced asthma or a history of it must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, children under 2 years of age, patients with a bleeding tendency, patients with or a history of liver disorder, kidney disorder, or blood disorders, those with a history of peptic ulcer, patients with bronchial asthma or abnormal cardiac function, those who have experienced hypersensitivity, elderly people, pregnant women, and nursing mothers should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If pain or fever persists or worsens, or if new symptoms appear, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Without instructions from a doctor or pharmacist, adults must not take it for pain for 10 days or longer and children must not take it for 5 days or longer, and it must not be taken for fever for 3 days or longer.
  • Children and elderly people should take the minimum necessary amount and watch for adverse reactions.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms such as difficulty breathing, reddening of the whole body, angioedema, or urticaria, or an asthma attack, thrombocytopenia, granulocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, methemoglobinemia, decreased platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), or hypersensitivity symptoms such as cyanosis, facial swelling, sweating, or low blood pressure, or nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation, rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), elevated AST, elevated ALT, or fixed drug eruption occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • People who have taken barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol should not take this medicine.
  • Do not take it together with other anti-inflammatory analgesics.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients on long-term warfarin and patients taking lithium or thiazide diuretics should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients who have or have had hypersensitivity to this medicine, by people who have had an asthma attack after taking this medicine, another antipyretic analgesic or a cold remedy, by children under 2 years of age and infants under 3 months of age, or by patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia or high anion gap metabolic acidosis appears, if symptoms of shock rarely appear (urticaria, swelling and a feeling of tightness in the chest right after taking it, together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat and difficulty breathing), or if asthma, generalized languor, jaundice, interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.), pseudoaldosteronism (reduced urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heavy eyelids, stiffening of the hands, a rise in blood pressure or headache, etc.) or myopathy (languor, cramp of the limbs, paralysis) appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take it together with antitussives (medicines that stop coughing) and expectorants (phlegm medicines), other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, oral medicines containing an antihistamine (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, allergy medicines), or flucloxacillin.

How to apply it

Apply it to the affected area (the diseased site) once a day. Soak the area in warm water, dry it completely, and gently rub the surface of the wart, corn, or callus with a pumice stone or a nail file to remove the hard skin. Using the applicator provided, carefully apply a few drops of this medicine to the affected area, letting each drop dry before applying the next. Be careful to apply it with the applicator only to the affected area, and for warts on the sole of the foot, cover with an adhesive plaster and leave it for 24 hours.   • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine, children under 2 years of age, and patients with diabetes or peripheral circulatory disorders must not use this medicine, and it must not be used on the face, in skin folds (overlapping skin), on the anogenital area, around the eyes, on mucous membranes, on moles, birthmarks, hairy warts, or other skin lesions.

  • Use it well away from the eyes and mucous membranes.
  • To avoid irritating the surrounding normal skin, apply it carefully only to warts, flat warts, corns, and calluses.
  • Be careful not to inhale the vapor.

Possible side effects

  • If severe or persistent pain and irritation occur, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Rarely, temporary blemishes may appear on the skin.

  • If any of the following appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rarely shock (chest discomfort, chills, difficulty breathing, fall in blood pressure, etc.); blood disorders such as aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time) and eosinophilia; peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, or very rarely dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal distension and constipation; Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome) or toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome); drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency; acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis; jaundice and increases in GOT, GPT and AL-P; induction of an asthma attack; urticaria, eczema, purpura, occasionally rash and itching; rarely visual disturbance such as blurred or dim vision, hearing loss, tinnitus and abnormal taste; aseptic meningitis, severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever or disturbance of consciousness; fall in blood pressure, rise in blood pressure and palpitations; acute renal failure, oliguria and hematuria together with proteinuria and increases in BUN and blood creatinine; hyperkalemia, reduced urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath and languor; acute pulmonary edema; occasionally periorbital edema; and very rarely malaise, fever and nosebleed.

Interactions

  • Do not use it together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when using it together with glucocorticoids, alcohol, digoxin, phenytoin, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, sulfonylureas, diuretics, antihypertensive medicines, ACE inhibitors, furosemide, aspirin, lithium, methotrexate, or coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin).

Oral medicine (MFDS 201309433)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201309433. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold (sore throat, chills (feeling cold and shivering), fever, headache, joint pain, muscle pain).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold (sore throat, chills (feeling cold and shivering), fever

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201309433. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults and those aged 15 years and older take 1 packet per dose, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. If necessary, take it at bedtime, and keep the interval between doses at 4 hours.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious and potentially fatal skin reactions such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.
  • If a severe skin adverse reaction such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis occurs, stop taking it and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, children under 2 years of age, and people who are taking an MAO inhibitor (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian drugs, etc.) or who stopped taking one within the past 2 weeks should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, people in whom symptoms of ischemic colitis (sudden abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, etc.) appear in connection with the pseudoephedrine component, people with an allergic constitution, people who have experienced allergic symptoms from medicines (e.g., fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), patients with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, edema, or gastroduodenal ulcer, elderly people, people who are physically weak, people with a high fever, people whose gastrointestinal problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain persist or recur or who have ulcers or bleeding problems, and pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after 5 to 6 doses, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration exactly.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, or, rarely, shock symptoms (urticaria and chest tightness right after taking the medicine, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing, etc.), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash and redness and burn-like blisters appearing on the skin over the whole body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes), asthma, general languor, jaundice, interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, and fever), decreased urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heavy eyelids, stiffening of the hands, raised blood pressure or headache, or myopathy (weakness, cramps in the limbs, paralysis, etc.) occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take together with antitussives and expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol, potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, etacrynic acid) or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide), diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, or steroids.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.

This medicine is used for the local treatment of candidal vaginitis, trichomonal vaginitis, vaginitis caused by non-specific and mixed infection and preparation before obstetric and gynecological surgery, and for germicidal vaginal washing, local washing and deodorizing.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Vaginal medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for the local treatment of candidal vaginitis, trichomonal vaginitis, vaginitis caused by non-spec

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199700636. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to insert it

Dilute 30 mL of povidone-iodine 10% (available iodine 1%) in about 1 L of warm water and wash the inside and the outside of the vagina 1 to 2 times a day. For germicidal vaginal washing, local washing and deodorizing, wash 1 to 2 times a week.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be used by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by patients with thyroid dysfunction (especially nodular goiter, endemic goiter, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, etc.), by patients with renal failure, by newborns and infants under 6 months of age, by patients with dermatitis herpetiformis, or by patients before or after radioactive iodine treatment.
  • Before using this medicine, patients in a serious condition (burn patients, etc.), patients who have had a thyroid disease, patients who have had renal failure, and pregnant or breast-feeding women should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If it has been used right before delivery, wash the newborn's eyes and bathe the baby as soon as possible after the delivery so that the medicine does not remain on the skin.
  • Do not use it for the eyes or internally.
  • If the undiluted solution gets into the eyes, rinse them out immediately with clean water.
  • Do not mix it with other preparations for use.
  • When this medicine is used on a patient with extensive burns, provide sufficient fluids.
  • Because this medicine has a spermicidal action, do not use it if pregnancy is desired.

Possible side effects

  • Anaphylactoid symptoms (difficulty breathing, flushing, urticaria, etc.) and hypersensitivity in the form of iododerma may rarely appear, pain, itching, a feeling of irritation, rash, redness and dermatitis may occasionally appear, and a burning sensation, skin ulcer, contact dermatitis and skin discoloration may rarely appear.

Interactions

  • Do not use this medicine together with hydrogen peroxide.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when using it together with lithium, chlorhexidine, sulfadiazine and silver compounds, alkalis, preparations containing mercury, or enzyme-based wound treatments.
  • This medicine may damage latex or rubber products such as condoms and vaginal contraceptive diaphragms.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to supply vitamins A, B1, B2, B6, C, D, and E during physical fatigue, pregnancy and breastfeeding

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201902565. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Children aged 8 years and older and adults take 2 tablets as 1 dose, 2 times a day, and children aged 36 months or older and under 8 years take 1 tablet as 1 dose, 2 times a day. Let the tablet dissolve in the mouth or chew it before swallowing.

Warning

  • Taking 5,000 IU or more of vitamin A a day may cause congenital malformations.
  • Women within 3 months of pregnancy or who may be pregnant must not take it.
  • An overdose in children aged 6 years or younger may cause death from iron poisoning, so keep it out of the reach of children.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypercalcemia (a condition in which calcium is present in excess in the blood), sarcoidosis (a systemic inflammatory disease of unknown cause), kidney disease, or hypersensitivity to this medicine, infants under 12 months of age, patients with hemochromatosis (a disease in which iron is deposited in the liver and pancreas because of abnormal iron metabolism), hemosiderosis, non-iron-deficiency anemia, kidney stones, or severe renal failure, and patients with genetic problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants under 1 year of age, children who get plenty of sunlight and eat a normal diet, patients with hyperoxaluria (a condition in which an excessive amount of oxalate is excreted in the urine), pregnant women and women who may be pregnant, nursing mothers, premature infants, infants, patients with gastrointestinal diseases such as peptic ulcer, chronic ulcerative colitis, or localized [appearing in a specific area] colitis, and those with cardiac and circulatory dysfunction, kidney [renal] disorder, hypoproteinemia, gout, or a history of kidney stones should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • When giving it to children, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • It may turn the urine yellow and affect clinical laboratory test values.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it for about 1 month, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If nausea, vomiting, itching, dry and rough skin, painful joint swelling, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, constipation, rash, redness (congested and reddened), loose stools, low blood pressure, facial flushing, irregular heartbeat, hives, photosensitivity reactions, abdominal or stomach pain, convulsions, fever, coma, red spots, asystole (cardiac arrest), depression of central nervous system function, gastrointestinal disorders, digestive disorders, upper abdominal pain, pulmonary edema, or symptoms such as menstruation coming earlier than expected, the flow gradually becoming heavier, or bleeding lasting for a long time occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with phosphates, calcium salts, oral (taken by mouth) tetracycline preparations, antacids, or levodopa.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking it together with oral (taken by mouth) contraceptives containing estrogen, antialdosterone agents, triamterene, or cardiac glycosides.
  • Avoid teas containing tannin, such as green tea and black tea, while taking it and before and after taking it.

How it works

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint diseas

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 198700315. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200-600 mg at a time, 3-4 times a day. Up to a maximum of 3,200 mg a day may be administered. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30-40 mg per kg of body weight at a time, 3 to 4 times a day. For mild to moderate pain and colds, adults take 200-400 mg at a time, 3 to 4 times a day. The dose may be increased or decreased appropriately according to age and symptoms. Children 11 to 14 years of age take 200 to 250 mg (10 to 12.5 mL) at a time, children 7 to 10 years of age take 150 to 200 mg (7.5 to 10 mL) at a time, children 3 to 6 years of age take 100 to 150 mg (5 to 7.5 mL) at a time, and children 1 to 2 years of age take 50 to 100 mg (2.5 to 5 mL) at a time, 3 to 4 times a day.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, severe blood abnormalities, severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma, patients who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, breastfeeding women, patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Do not take more than the recommended dose.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with blood abnormalities or a bleeding tendency, patients with liver cirrhosis, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, heart disease, high blood pressure, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people, children under 2 years of age, pregnant women, and patients with chickenpox should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • When taking it for a cold, take it for no more than 5 days as a rule, and without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist do not take it for pain for 10 days or more (adults) or 5 days or more (children), and do not take it for fever for 3 days or more.

Possible side effects

  • If shock (difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, etc.), blood disorders such as decreased hematocrit, decreased hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function and eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stool, gastritis, pancreatitis, vomiting of blood, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, oral ulcer, constipation, black stool, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, exfoliative dermatitis, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, hepatitis, jaundice, abnormal liver function, liver disorder, hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reactions, asthma attacks, urticaria, eczema, purple spots, visual disturbance, hearing loss, ringing in the ears, taste disturbance, vertigo, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness, aseptic meningitis or meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever or impaired consciousness), acute renal failure, decreased urination, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and accompanying shortness of breath, listlessness, swelling around the eyes, facial swelling, malaise, fever, nosebleed, swelling, or peripheral edema occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy should not take this medicine, and do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics.
  • Before taking this medicine, people taking low-dose aspirin or ACE inhibitors and patients taking lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201801818. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

Use this medicine in the following order. Remove the applicator from its packaging and hold it with the sponge facing downwards. Do not touch the sponge part of the applicator. Squeeze the applicator firmly only once so that the ampoule breaks and the solution comes out, and leave the broken ampoule inside the applicator. For the 26 mL product, squeeze the lever on the handle firmly, and for the other products squeeze both wings firmly. Do not squeeze or press the wings repeatedly in order to wet the sponge quickly. Press and release the sponge against the treatment area until the solution is visible on the skin, wetting the sponge and completely wetting the treatment area with the solution. For a dry surgical site (e.g. the abdomen or an arm), once the solution is visible on the skin, rub gently back and forth for 30 seconds to treat that area. For a moist surgical site (e.g. the groin fold), rub gently back and forth repeatedly for about 2 minutes. Let the area to which the solution has been applied dry completely in the air, and do not wipe the solution off. Discard the applicator after a single use, together with any remaining solution that was not used on the treatment area. It is not necessary to use the entire amount.

Precautions for use

  • People with hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine, isopropanol, or Yellow No. 5 and infants aged 2 months or younger should not use this medicine.
  • Do not use this medicine for disinfecting surgical instruments, or on nervous tissue (e.g., brain or spinal cord tissue), the eyes, ears, mouth, mucous membranes, genital mucous membranes, open wounds, or torn or damaged skin, or for general washing of the skin.
  • Before using this medicine, people with hypersensitivity to other medicines, people who have experienced allergic diseases such as asthma or who have a family history of them, people with hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine preparations, and people with a drug-hypersensitive constitution should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Use it externally only on intact skin.
  • Contact with the eyes may cause corneal damage, so be careful not to let it get into the eyes; if it does get in, rinse thoroughly with clean water immediately.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms (nausea, malaise, cold sweat, dizziness, a stifling feeling, difficulty breathing, redness, a sudden drop in blood pressure, urticaria, angioedema, etc.), occasionally rash, photosensitization, irritation, sensitization, erythema or inflammation, itching, dry and thinly peeling skin, local pain at the application site, or local skin reactions, or very rarely rash (e.g., erythematous, papular, or maculopapular), blisters, small blisters at the application site, a burning sensation of the skin, dermatitis, eczema, chemical burns in newborns, eye irritation, congestion, impaired vision, or eye damage occurs, stop using this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Those aged 15 years and older take 1 packet (20 ml) at a time, those aged 11 years to under 15 years take 2/3 packet at a time, those aged 7 years to under 11 years take 1/2 packet at a time, those aged 3 years to under 7 years take 1/3 packet at a time, and those aged 2 years to under 3 years take 1/4 packet at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.   • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.

  • Do not take more than the maximum daily amount of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).

Precautions for use

  • Those with hypersensitivity to this medicine or a history of it, people who have experienced asthma when taking this medicine or its ingredients, other antipyretic analgesics, or cold medicines, infants under 3 months of age, and children under 2 years of age must not take this medicine.

  • Drowsiness may occur while taking it.
  • Avoid driving a car or operating machinery.
  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, swelling, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, or insomnia occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • While taking this medicine, do not take antitussives and expectorants, other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives or oral medicines containing an antihistamine.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

After the hair and the scalp are completely dry, apply 0.5 to 1 mL of this medicine to the affected area only, twice a day (morning and evening), for at least 4 months, and do not let the total daily amount exceed 2 mL.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be used by women, people under 18 years of age, patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, patients with a cardiovascular disease (coronary artery disease, arrhythmia, congestive heart failure, valvular heart disease, treated or untreated high blood pressure, low blood pressure), patients who have no hereditary factor for hair loss, patients with sudden patchy hair loss, patients with a scalp abnormality such as erythema, inflammation, infection, irritation or pain of the scalp, psoriasis or sunburn, patients with hair loss of unknown cause, patients who are using another medicine for the scalp, patients who have shaved the scalp, or patients who tolerate the 2 % strength poorly.
  • Before using this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the user is elderly, has edema, has thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism), has local exfoliation, dermatitis, psoriasis of the scalp or a severe burn, or has a history of heart disease.
  • Use this medicine externally only and do not use it on any area other than the scalp.
  • Do not use an occlusive dressing.
  • Because this medicine may cause burning and irritation of the eyes, be careful to keep it out of the eyes, and if it touches a sensitive area such as the eyes, broken skin or a mucous membrane, rinse it off immediately with clean water.
  • Use hair styling products after this medicine has dried, and when using it in the evening, use it 2 to 4 hours before bedtime so that it can dry.
  • Because circulation of air over the scalp may reduce the effect of this medicine, do not use a hair dryer to speed up its drying.

Possible side effects

  • If any of the following appears, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: itching, scaling, erythema, redness, dermatitis, dry skin, excessive hair growth at sites other than the area where this medicine was applied (facial hair growth in women), folliculitis, local irritation including a burning sensation and skin eruption, exfoliation, hair loss, skin abscess, acne, nail disorder, seborrhea, eczema, hair abnormality, bronchitis, upper respiratory tract infection, sinusitis, difficulty breathing, occasional diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, change in blood pressure, change in pulse, palpitations, increased heart rate, pericardial effusion, pericarditis, embolism, tachycardia, worsening of pre-existing angina or induction of angina in a person with undiagnosed coronary artery disease, shortness of breath, fracture, back pain, tendinitis, pain, neuritis (including polyneuritis), weakness, dizziness, headache, feeling dazed, fainting, hepatitis, edema, kidney stones, inflammation and fluid retention, fever, urticaria, allergic rhinitis, systemic erythema and facial swelling, chills, eye irritation, bitter taste, otitis (especially otitis externa), change in taste, visual disturbance, erectile dysfunction, stabbing pain, or sudden unexplained weight gain.

Interactions

  • Do not use it together with other medicines for the scalp, medicines that promote absorption through the skin (for example topical corticosteroids, retinoids, petrolatum, dithranol), or vasodilators (for example guanethidine, etc.).

How to take it

Adults and children aged 12 years and older take 10 mg a day; children aged 2 to under 12 years take 10 mg a day if they weigh 30 kg or more and 5 mg a day if they weigh less than 30 kg, taken 1 time a day. Patients who are sensitive to adverse reactions take it in divided doses in the morning and evening. The dose may be increased or decreased appropriately according to age and symptoms.   • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or to hydroxyzine or piperazine derivatives or those who have experienced it, patients with renal failure, pregnant women and women who may be pregnant, breastfeeding women, infants under 2 years of age, and patients with fructose intolerance should not take this medicine.

  • Do not take more than the specified dose when driving or operating machinery.
  • It is advisable not to take this medicine for 3 to 5 days before an allergen intradermal skin test.

  • If drowsiness, headache, vasculitis, photosensitivity, dizziness, joint pain, pharyngitis, cough, nosebleed, bronchospasm, hearing abnormalities, visual abnormalities, occasionally elevated BUN, glycosuria, or blood in the urine, or rarely difficulty urinating, bedwetting, or urinary retention occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take this medicine together with theophylline or ritonavir.

How it works

This medicine is used as temporary adjunctive therapy for bacterial gingivitis (inflammation of the gums), bacterial inf

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201802940. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

Before using this medicine, brush your teeth and rinse your mouth with plenty of water. 2 to 3 times a day, after meals and after brushing, apply an appropriate amount of this medicine directly to the inflamed area in the mouth using the nozzle, leave it for about 1 minute, and then spit it out. Warning

  • Do not use it for a long period, because it may cause an imbalance of the normal bacterial flora in the mouth.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine must not use this medicine.
  • Before using this medicine, patients with bronchial asthma or other respiratory diseases related to airway hypersensitivity, patients with allergic diseases, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, and children under 18 years of age should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not take it orally.
  • Do not use it on or around the eyes or ears, and if it is applied there by mistake, rinse thoroughly with water.
  • Do not use it on tissue with poor blood circulation, on wounds and ulcers (ulceration), or on externally non-bleeding wound areas (corrosive exfoliative changes).
  • If you apply too much of this medicine, wash it off with water.
  • It may cause discoloration of oral surfaces such as the tooth surfaces, dental prostheses, and the underside of the tongue.

Possible side effects

  • If hypersensitivity reactions (rash, swelling of the lips, tongue, throat, or face, difficulty breathing) rarely occur, stop using this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Temporary peeling changes of the mucous membrane, such as a specific lesion of the oral mucosa, reduced taste, and a reversible numb state of the tongue may occur.

Interactions

  • This medicine does not combine well with soap or with the anionic substances that are common ingredients of toothpaste, so do not use this medicine at the same time as those ingredients; after brushing your teeth, rinse your mouth with plenty of water and use this medicine at least 5 minutes later.
  • After using this medicine, refrain from eating food or drinking beverages containing sugar.
  • Sugar can impair the effect of this medicine.

How it works

This drug is used for reducing fever when fever occurs due to acute upper respiratory tract infection.

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 200608160. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Children aged 6 months and older take 0.4 to 0.6 mL/kg (5 to 7 mg/kg) per dose as needed at intervals of 4 to 6 hours, not exceeding a maximum of 4 doses a day (28 mg/kg). If the body weight is known, it is more appropriate to take the dose based on body weight, so refer to the approved product information for the recommended doses by age group.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.
  • Taking this medicine may cause serious and potentially fatal gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, peptic ulcer, severe blood disorders, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, severe heart failure, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma or a history of it, patients with or a history of asthma, urticaria, or allergy caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients being treated for pain before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, and pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and nursing mothers must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, those with a history of peptic ulcer, patients with or a history of blood disorders, patients with a bleeding tendency, patients with or a history of liver disorder or kidney disorder, patients with heart failure, high blood pressure, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people and children, patients with stomach cancer, and people taking low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If any of the following occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rarely shock (chills, difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, etc.), aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stool, gastritis, pancreatitis; occasionally loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort; very rarely dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, constipation, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome) or Lyell's syndrome (toxic epidermal necrolysis); drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency, jaundice, elevated GOT, GPT and AL-P, induction of asthma attacks, urticaria, eczema, purpura; occasionally rash, itching, visual disturbances such as misty vision and dimmed vision, hearing loss, tinnitus, taste disturbance, aseptic meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness), autoimmune diseases (SLE, MCTD); rarely drop in blood pressure, rise in blood pressure, palpitations; rarely acute renal failure (oliguria, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, decreased urine volume, generalized edema, shortness of breath, listlessness), heart failure, Conn's syndrome of unknown frequency, occasionally periorbital edema, and very rarely malaise, fever, or nosebleed.

  • Do not use together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.

Children aged 2 to 6 years take 5 mL at a time and children aged 6 to 12 years take 10 mL at a time, every 4 to 6 hours. Do not take 4 or more doses in 24 hours.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Topical medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for disinfection of the patient's skin before surgery or before insertion of a syringe needle or a

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201801818. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

Use this medicine in the following order. Remove the applicator from its packaging and hold it with the sponge facing downwards. Do not touch the sponge part of the applicator. Squeeze the applicator firmly only once so that the ampoule breaks and the solution comes out, and leave the broken ampoule inside the applicator. For the 26 mL product, squeeze the lever on the handle firmly, and for the other products squeeze both wings firmly. Do not squeeze or press the wings repeatedly in order to wet the sponge quickly. Press and release the sponge against the treatment area until the solution is visible on the skin, wetting the sponge and completely wetting the treatment area with the solution. For a dry surgical site (e.g. the abdomen or an arm), once the solution is visible on the skin, rub gently back and forth for 30 seconds to treat that area. For a moist surgical site (e.g. the groin fold), rub gently back and forth repeatedly for about 2 minutes. Let the area to which the solution has been applied dry completely in the air, and do not wipe the solution off. Discard the applicator after a single use, together with any remaining solution that was not used on the treatment area. It is not necessary to use the entire amount.

Precautions for use

  • People with hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine, isopropanol, or Yellow No. 5 and infants aged 2 months or younger should not use this medicine.
  • Do not use this medicine for disinfecting surgical instruments, or on nervous tissue (e.g., brain or spinal cord tissue), the eyes, ears, mouth, mucous membranes, genital mucous membranes, open wounds, or torn or damaged skin, or for general washing of the skin.
  • Before using this medicine, people with hypersensitivity to other medicines, people who have experienced allergic diseases such as asthma or who have a family history of them, people with hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine preparations, and people with a drug-hypersensitive constitution should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Use it externally only on intact skin.
  • Contact with the eyes may cause corneal damage, so be careful not to let it get into the eyes; if it does get in, rinse thoroughly with clean water immediately.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms (nausea, malaise, cold sweat, dizziness, a stifling feeling, difficulty breathing, redness, a sudden drop in blood pressure, urticaria, angioedema, etc.), occasionally rash, photosensitization, irritation, sensitization, erythema or inflammation, itching, dry and thinly peeling skin, local pain at the application site, or local skin reactions, or very rarely rash (e.g., erythematous, papular, or maculopapular), blisters, small blisters at the application site, a burning sensation of the skin, dermatitis, eczema, chemical burns in newborns, eye irritation, congestion, impaired vision, or eye damage occurs, stop using this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200-600 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. Up to a maximum of 3,200 mg a day may be taken. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30 to 40 mg per kg of body weight per dose, in 3 to 4 divided doses a day. For mild to moderate pain and for colds, adults take 200 to 400 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. The dose may be increased or decreased as appropriate according to age and symptoms. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years take 200 to 250 mg (10 to 12.5 mL) per dose, those aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg (7.5 to 10 mL) per dose, those aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg (5 to 7.5 mL) per dose, and those aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg (2.5 to 5 mL) per dose, 3 to 4 times a day, and it is advisable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years may take up to 1,000 mg (50 mL) a day, those aged 7 to 10 years up to 800 mg (40 mL), those aged 3 to 6 years up to 600 mg (30 mL), and those aged 1 to 2 years up to 400 mg (20 mL).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, severe blood abnormalities, severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma, patients who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, breastfeeding women, patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Do not take more than the recommended dose.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with blood abnormalities or a bleeding tendency, patients with liver cirrhosis, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, heart disease, high blood pressure, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people, children under 2 years of age, pregnant women, and patients with chickenpox should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • When taking it for a cold, take it for no more than 5 days as a rule, and without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist do not take it for pain for 10 days or more (adults) or 5 days or more (children), and do not take it for fever for 3 days or more.

  • If shock (difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, etc.), decreased hematocrit, decreased hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, decreased platelet function, or blood disorders such as eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation (a hole forming), ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, vomiting of blood, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, oral ulcer, constipation, black stools, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, exfoliative dermatitis, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, hepatitis, jaundice, liver function abnormalities, hepatic impairment, hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reaction, asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purple spots, visual disturbance, deafness, ringing in the ears, taste disturbance, dizziness, drowsiness, lightheadedness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness, aseptic meningitis or meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever or disturbance of consciousness), acute renal failure, decreased urination, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN or blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and accompanying shortness of breath, listlessness, Kounis syndrome of unknown frequency, swelling around the eyes, facial swelling, malaise, fever, nosebleed, swelling, or peripheral edema occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease), gastrointestinal obstruction, abdominal pain of unknown cause, or a low-galactose diet (galactosemia), patients with gastrointestinal perforation or a risk of it, and patients with genetic problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), fever and pain due to a cold, low back pain, dysmenorrhea, post-operative pain and ankylosing spondylitis, headache, toothache, muscle pain, neuralgia, acute gout, psoriatic arthritis, soft tissue injury (sprain, contusion), and non-articular rheumatic diseases (tendinitis, tenosynovitis, bursitis).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint diseas

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 198901310. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200-600 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. Up to a maximum of 3,200 mg a day may be taken. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30 to 40 mg per kg of body weight per dose, in 3 to 4 divided doses a day. For mild to moderate pain and for colds, adults take 200 to 400 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. The dose may be increased or decreased as appropriate according to age and symptoms. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years take 200 to 250 mg (10 to 12.5 mL) per dose, those aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg (7.5 to 10 mL) per dose, those aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg (5 to 7.5 mL) per dose, and those aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg (2.5 to 5 mL) per dose, 3 to 4 times a day, and it is advisable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years may take up to 1,000 mg (50 mL) a day, those aged 7 to 10 years up to 800 mg (40 mL), those aged 3 to 6 years up to 600 mg (30 mL), and those aged 1 to 2 years up to 400 mg (20 mL).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, severe blood abnormalities, severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma, patients who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, breastfeeding women, patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Do not take more than the recommended dose.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with blood abnormalities or a bleeding tendency, patients with liver cirrhosis, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, heart disease, high blood pressure, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people, children under 2 years of age, pregnant women, and patients with chickenpox should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • When taking it for a cold, take it for no more than 5 days as a rule, and without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist do not take it for pain for 10 days or more (adults) or 5 days or more (children), and do not take it for fever for 3 days or more.

Possible side effects

How to take it

Adults and children aged 8 years and older take 20 to 40 ml (1 to 2 packets) a day, based on a package unit of 1 packet (20 ml). Depending on symptoms, children in particular may take 20 ml (1 packet) every other day. Dissolve 20 ml (1 packet) of this medicine in water to make 50 ml and then take it. It is recommended to take it in the morning. For children from 6 months to 7 years of age, based on a package unit of 1 packet (8 ml), children 6 months to 1 year of age take 8 ml (1 packet) a day, children 1 to 4 years of age take 8 to 16 ml (1 to 2 packets) a day, and children 4 to 7 years of age take 16 to 32 ml (2 to 4 packets) a day. If 1 packet (8 ml) a day is taken, take it in the morning; if more than 1 packet (8 ml) a day is taken, divide the dose between morning and evening. Dissolve 8 ml (1 packet) of this medicine in water to make 50 ml and then take it.

Precautions for use

  • People who are hypersensitive to this medicine and patients with inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, etc.), toxic megacolon, intestinal perforation, intestinal obstruction, intestinal stricture, or abdominal pain of unknown cause must not take this medicine.
  • Do not take this medicine for a long period without a doctor's judgment.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if you are pregnant, may be pregnant, or are breastfeeding, if you have acute constipation not caused by a change in lifestyle habits (such as acute constipation accompanied by pain, fever, or abdominal distension), if you have irritable bowel syndrome, or if you have a hypersensitivity reaction to macrogol (polyethylene glycol).
  • Do not give this medicine to children for more than 3 months.

Possible side effects

  • In adults, if abdominal pain and bloating, diarrhea, or nausea occurs, uncommonly vomiting or urgent bowel movements, with unknown frequency fecal incontinence, electrolyte disturbances (hyponatremia, hypokalemia, etc.), dehydration, or erythema, or very rarely hypersensitivity reactions (itching, rash, facial swelling, angioedema, hives, anaphylaxis, shock, etc.), stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • In children, if abdominal pain, diarrhea and pain around the anus caused by diarrhea occurs, uncommonly vomiting, abdominal bloating, or nausea, or very rarely hypersensitivity reactions (hypersensitivity, angioedema, hives, rash, itching, etc.), stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, heart failure, or high blood pressure, patients with bronchial asthma, patients with asthma, urticaria, or allergy caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics or those who have experienced it, patients being treated for pain before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, and pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with hypersensitivity, peptic ulcer, blood abnormalities, a bleeding tendency, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, high blood pressure, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, gastric cancer, or Crohn's disease, elderly people, children, and people who take low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • If rarely shock (difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, etc.), aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, decreased platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome) or toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms of unknown frequency (DRESS syndrome), acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, induction of an asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, or purpura occurs, or occasionally rash or itching, or rarely loss of vision, visual disturbances such as scotoma, aseptic meningitis, acute renal failure, oliguria, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN or blood creatinine, or hyperkalemia occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If occasionally loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, or periorbital edema occurs, or rarely jaundice, elevated GOT, GPT, or ALP, hearing loss, tinnitus, taste disturbance, drop in blood pressure, rise in blood pressure, palpitations, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and accompanying shortness of breath, listlessness, or acute pulmonary edema occurs, or very rarely dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, constipation, malaise, fever, or nosebleed occurs, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not use this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when using it together with glucocorticoids, alcohol, digoxin, phenytoin, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, sulfonylureas, the combined use of diuretics and antihypertensives, ACE inhibitors, furosemide, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, or coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin, etc.).

Why this one

Who should ask first

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and older and adults take 1 bottle at a time, those aged 11 years to under 15 years take 2/3 bottle at a time, those aged 7 years to under 11 years take 1/2 bottle at a time, those aged 3 years to under 7 years take 1/3 bottle at a time, and those aged 1 year to under 3 years take 1/4 bottle at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. Allow 4 hours between doses.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, in patients taking acetaminophen, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported, and if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily amount of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products that contain acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, and infants under 3 months of age and children under 2 years of age must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the user is an infant or a child under 15 years of age who has or is suspected of having chickenpox or influenza; if the user is a child under 2 years of age for whom it is strictly necessary; if you are pregnant, may be pregnant, or are breastfeeding; if you are elderly or frail; if you have an allergic constitution or have experienced allergic symptoms (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.); or if you have liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, swelling, gastroduodenal ulcer, high fever, stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort or stomach pain, ulcers, or bleeding problems.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • When giving it to a child, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking 5 to 6 doses, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If rash, redness, itching, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, swelling, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling, and chest tightness immediately after taking the medicine together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweats, and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (severe symptoms with high fever, rash and redness, and burn-like blisters appearing on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes), asthma, general listlessness, jaundice, interstitial pneumonia (with cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever), decreased urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, rising blood pressure or headache, or myopathy (weakness, cramps in the limbs, paralysis, etc.) occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take together with other products containing acetaminophen, MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian drugs, etc.), antitussives and expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
